## 5. Dose response: a monotone staircase that saturates

**Theorem 5.1 (Monotonicity in the bound).** If $B \le B'$ then $k(B) \mid k(B')$, and hence $\gcd(m,k(B)) \mid \gcd(m,k(B'))$ and $\gcd(m,k(B)) \le \gcd(m,k(B'))$ for $m \ne 0$.

*Proof sketch.* Prime by prime: for a prime $r \le B$ we have $r \le B'$ and $\lfloor \log_r B\rfloor \le \lfloor\log_r B'\rfloor$; for $B < r \le B'$ the exponent rises from $0$. $\square$

**Theorem 5.2 (No dose response).** Let $m, B, B' \ne 0$. If for every prime $q \mid m$ and every $1 \le j \le v_q(m)$ the conditions $q^j \le B$ and $q^j \le B'$ are equivalent — that is, no prime power dividing $m$ separates $B$ from $B'$ — then
$$\gcd(m,k(B)) = \gcd(m,k(B')).$$

*Proof sketch.* Compare exponents. For a prime $r \mid m$ the exponent of $r$ in $\gcd(m,k(B))$ is $\min(v_r(m), \lfloor\log_r B\rfloor)$ if $r \le B$ and $0$ otherwise. The hypothesis at $j=1$ makes the conditions $r \le B$ and $r \le B'$ equivalent; and the key elementary fact is that $\min(v,\lfloor\log_r B\rfloor)$ equals the largest $j \le v$ with $r^{j} \le B$, so the hypothesis for $1 \le j \le v_r(m)$ makes the two minima equal. Primes not dividing $m$ contribute $0$ on both sides. $\square$

Theorem 5.2 is the exact statement matching the recorded flatness of success rates in the budget fraction. Rates are piecewise constant in the bound, with jumps only at the (few) prime powers dividing the order.

**Theorem 5.3 (Saturation).** For $m, B \ne 0$: $\gcd(m,k(B)) = m$ if and only if $m$ is $B$-powersmooth.

*Proof sketch.* $\gcd(m,k(B)) = m \iff m \mid k(B) \iff$ powersmoothness, by Theorem 3.2. $\square$

Beyond powersmoothness, additional bound buys nothing: the staircase has topped out at rate $1$.

**Theorem 5.4 (Exact jump formula).** For $m \ne 0$ and $q$ prime,
$$\gcd\bigl(m, k(B,q)\bigr) \;=\; \gcd\bigl(m, k(B,q-1)\bigr)\cdot q^{\min\left(v_q(m),\, \lfloor \log_q B\rfloor\right)}.$$
In particular the count is unchanged when $q \nmid m$ or when $q > B$.

*Proof sketch.* Compare exponents at each prime $r$. At $r = q$: the left side carries $\min(v_q(m), \lfloor \log_q B\rfloor)$ (as $q \le q$), the right side $0 + \min(v_q(m),\lfloor\log_q B\rfloor)$ (as $q \not\le q-1$). At $r \ne q$ the conditions $r \le q$ and $r \le q-1$ agree and the extra factor contributes $0$. $\square$

Theorem 5.4 makes the staircase completely explicit: it is the partial-product sequence of the numbers $q^{\min(v_q(m), \lfloor\log_q B\rfloor)}$ over primes $q$ in increasing order, terminating (by Theorem 5.3) at the powersmooth part of $m$.

## 6. The long inert block: a pigeonhole obstruction to uniformity

Theorem 4.5 says the staircase has at most $\omega(m)$ jumps in $\pi(B)$ steps. A counting argument converts sparse jumps into a single long flat block.

**Lemma 6.1 (Same jump count implies same firing count).** For $C \le C' \le B$, if the number of jump primes $\le C$ equals the number of jump primes $\le C'$, then $\gcd(m,k(B,C)) = \gcd(m,k(B,C'))$.

*Proof sketch.* The two filtered sets are nested with equal cardinality, hence equal; so no prime divisor of $m$ lies in $(C,C']$, and Theorem 4.4 applies. $\square$

**Theorem 6.2 (Existence of a long inert block).** For $m, B \ne 0$ there is a set $S$ of schedule primes with
$$|S| \;\ge\; \frac{\pi(B)}{\omega(m)+1}$$
on which the firing count is constant: $\gcd(m,k(B,C)) = \gcd(m,k(B,C'))$ for all $C, C' \in S$.

*Proof sketch.* Map each schedule prime $C$ to the number of jump primes $\le C$, a value in $\{0,1,\dots,\omega(m)\}$ by Theorem 4.5. The schedule has $\pi(B)$ elements and the target has $\omega(m)+1$ values, so by pigeonhole some fiber has size at least $\pi(B)/(\omega(m)+1)$. Lemma 6.1 shows the firing count is constant on any fiber. $\square$

**Corollary 6.3.** If $\omega(m) \le 1$, at least half of the schedule is inert.

The uniform comparison distribution increases at every one of the $\pi(B)$ steps. A block of $\pi(B)/(\omega(m)+1)$ steps on which the empirical cumulative distribution is exactly constant is precisely the structural feature a Kolmogorov–Smirnov-type statistic responds to. Theorem 6.2 does not by itself produce a numerical lower bound on the sup-distance to uniform — that requires knowing where the block sits, not merely how long it is (see §10) — but it identifies the obstruction.

## 7. Controls, amplification, and the collision baseline

### 7.1 The control channel

**Theorem 7.1 (Collapse when order completion is impossible).** If every prime factor of $m$ exceeds $B$, then $\gcd(m,k(B)) = 1$, i.e. $|F(m,k(B))| = 1$: only the identity fires, and the order-completion rate is exactly $1/m$.

*Proof sketch.* By Theorem 4.2 the gcd is a powersmooth divisor of $m$; if it had a prime factor $q$, then $q \mid m$ and $q \le q^{v_q} \le B$, contradicting the hypothesis. So the gcd is $1$. $\square$

This is exactly the design logic of the experimental control: at the large factor $q$ of the modulus, $B \ll q$ forces the order-completion contribution down to $1/m$, so hits observed there measure the collision floor alone. The recorded separation — $9$–$16$ control hits versus $24$–$31$ signal hits per cell — is therefore an attribution of the excess to order completion, not an appeal to a model.

### 7.2 Rank-two groups

For a prime $p$, $E(\mathbb{F}_p) \cong \mathbb{Z}/m_1 \times \mathbb{Z}/m_2$ with $m_2 \mid m_1$ (possibly $m_2 = 1$).

**Theorem 7.2 (Firing count in a rank-two group).** The number of points of $\mathbb{Z}/m_1\times\mathbb{Z}/m_2$ annihilated by $k$ is $\gcd(m_1,k)\cdot\gcd(m_2,k)$.

*Proof sketch.* The firing set is the product $F(m_1,k)\times F(m_2,k)$; apply Theorem 4.1 to each factor. $\square$

**Corollary 7.3 (Rank two fires at least as often).** $\gcd(m_1 m_2, k) \le \gcd(m_1,k)\cdot\gcd(m_2,k)$.

*Proof sketch.* $\gcd(m_1m_2,k)$ divides $\gcd(m_1,k)\gcd(m_2,k)$, and the latter is positive. $\square$

Splitting the order into two cyclic factors can only enlarge the powersmooth part; the cyclic model is a conservative lower bound for real curves.

### 7.3 Multi-curve amplification

**Theorem 7.4 (Exact multi-curve count).** With $c$ independently chosen points of a cyclic group of order $m$, the number of $c$-tuples on which stage 1 fires at least once is exactly
$$m^{c} - \bigl(m - \gcd(m,k)\bigr)^{c},$$
so the success rate is exactly $1 - (1-\rho)^{c}$ with $\rho = \gcd(m,k)/m$.

*Proof sketch.* The complementary event "no coordinate fires" is a product set: each coordinate ranges over the $m - \gcd(m,k)$ non-firing residues, giving $(m-\gcd(m,k))^c$ tuples. Subtract from $m^c$. The rate identity is algebra. $\square$

Note that no independence *assumption* is made: this is a count of tuples in a product set, and independence is a consequence of the product structure rather than a hypothesis.

### 7.4 Against the collision heuristic

**Theorem 7.5 (Order completion beats the baseline).** For $m > 0$, if $\gcd(m, k(B)) > 1.44\,B$, then
$$1 - \exp\!\left(-\frac{1.44\,B}{m}\right) \;<\; \frac{\gcd(m,k(B))}{m}.$$

*Proof sketch.* $1 - e^{-x}\le x$ for all real $x$ (from $1 + t \le e^{t}$ at $t = -x$), so the baseline is at most $1.44 B/m$; the hypothesis gives $1.44 B/m < \gcd(m,k(B))/m$. $\square$

The folklore collision rate is thus not merely a different model — it is *dominated* by the exact order-completion rate whenever the powersmooth part of the order exceeds the linear threshold $1.44 B$. In the observed regime it is a floor, and the measured rates sit far above it.

## 8. A fully worked cell: $m = 720$, $B = 10$

Take $m = 720 = 2^4\cdot 3^2\cdot 5$ and $B = 10$. Then
$$k(10) = 2^{3}\cdot 3^{2}\cdot 5^{1}\cdot 7^{1} = 2520,\qquad \gcd(720, 2520) = 360 .$$

**The exact rate.** By Theorem 4.1, exactly $360$ of the $720$ residues fire: rate $1/2$. By Theorem 4.2, $360 = 2^3\cdot3^2\cdot5$ is the largest $10$-powersmooth divisor of $720$ — the factor $2^4 = 16 > 10$ is exactly what is lost.

**The staircase.** Advancing the cutoff through $1, 2, 3, 5, 7, 10$, the cumulative firing counts $\gcd(720, k(10,C))$ are
$$1,\quad 8,\quad 72,\quad 360,\quad 360,\quad 360 .$$
Each step matches Theorem 5.4: $2^{\min(4,3)} = 8$, then $\times 3^{\min(2,2)} = 9$, then $\times 5^{\min(1,1)} = 5$, then $\times 7^{\min(0,1)} = 1$. Two of the four schedule primes do nothing: $7$ because it does not divide $m$, and everything after $5$ because the count has saturated at the powersmooth part.

**Early fire.** $5\cdot\gcd(720, k(10,3)) = 5\cdot 72 = 360 = \gcd(720,k(10,10))$, and $2\cdot 360 = 720$: half of the whole group fires, and one fifth of all points that ever fire have already fired after only the first two of the four schedule primes. This is early fire in the exact sense of Corollary 3.5 and Theorem 4.7.

**Against the collision baseline.** The heuristic per-curve collision rate is at most $1.44\cdot 10/720 = 0.02$, while the true order-completion rate is $0.5$ — more than $25$ times larger. Theorem 7.5 applies since $\gcd(720,k(10)) = 360 > 14.4$.

**Multi-curve.** With $c = 3$ curves, Theorem 7.4 gives exactly $720^3 - 360^3$ successful triples, a rate of $1 - (1/2)^3 = 7/8 = 0.875$ — the scale of rate seen in the experimental cells at three curves.

---

## 9. Algorithmic consequences

Three of the results have direct operational content.

**9.1 Schedule pruning is bounded by the jump set.** By Theorem 4.5, only the primes dividing the group order can ever change the firing count. For a fixed unknown order, at most $\omega(m) \le \log_2 m$ of the $\pi(B)$ steps matter. One cannot identify them in advance — that is the factoring problem itself — but the structural fact bounds the achievable benefit of any adaptive schedule reordering: the useful steps are $O(\log m)$ in number, and by Theorem 3.4 the last of them is $\mathrm{lpf}(m)$.

**9.2 Budget allocation should be front-loaded.** Theorem 4.7 says everything but the large-prime part has already fired by any cutoff $L$. Empirically the median firing position lies in the first $10$–$30\%$ of the schedule. Under a fixed total budget, allocating trials to *more curves at a modest bound* rather than *fewer curves at a large bound* is favoured exactly when the staircase for a typical order is already saturated below the modest bound. Theorem 7.4 quantifies the trade: $c$ curves at rate $\rho$ give $1-(1-\rho)^c$ exactly.

**9.3 Dose response is not a tuning signal.** A practitioner who observes no rate change when raising $B$ should not conclude that the run is failing or that measurement noise dominates. Theorem 5.2 says exactly zero change is the *predicted* outcome unless the increase crosses a prime power dividing the order. Absence of dose response is evidence *for* order completion, not against it.

We record the two computational kernels used throughout.

**Algorithm A (staircase evaluation).** Given $m$ and $B$, compute the sequence $C \mapsto \gcd(m, k(B,C))$ over all primes $C \le B$ by sieving the primes up to $B$ ($O(B\log\log B)$), then maintaining a running product and gcd. Using Theorem 5.4, the update at $q$ is a multiplication by $q^{\min(v_q(m),\lfloor\log_q B\rfloor)}$, so the whole staircase costs $O(\pi(B)\log m)$ arithmetic operations without ever forming the (astronomically large) scalar $k(B)$.

**Algorithm B (firing position).** Given $m$ and $B$, decide firing and locate the firing position: factor $m$, test powersmoothness ($q^{v_q(m)} \le B$ for all $q \mid m$), and if it holds return $\mathrm{lpf}(m)$; the normalized position is $\pi(\mathrm{lpf}(m))/\pi(B)$. Correctness is Theorems 3.2 and 3.4.

---

## 10. Limitations: what is not provable at this generality

Two natural strengthenings of the empirical statements are *not* theorems at this level, and it is worth being precise about why.

**10.1 A distributional early-fire theorem.** The statement "the median normalized firing position is at most $0.3$" cannot be proved from arithmetic alone. For a single order $m$ the firing position is deterministic — it is $\pi(\mathrm{lpf}(m))/\pi(B)$ by Theorem 3.4 — so a median statement is a statement about a *family*, i.e. about the distribution of largest prime factors of powersmooth numbers in a range. That is Dickman-type analytic input (the density of integers whose largest prime factor is below $x^{1/u}$), and it is not available unconditionally in the form the experiment's operationalization requires. What survives unconditionally is the deterministic skeleton, Theorem 4.7: all but the large-prime part has already fired by cutoff $L$.

**10.2 A quantitative distance-to-uniform bound.** We prove the support-size version (Theorem 4.6) and the long-inert-block version (Theorem 6.2), which together make uniformity impossible. Converting a flat block of length $\ell$ into a lower bound on the Kolmogorov–Smirnov distance requires locating the block within the schedule: a flat run adjacent to the boundary contributes little sup-distance, while a flat run straddling the middle contributes about $\ell/(2\pi(B))$. Locating the block needs information about the position of the prime divisors of $m$ in the schedule, which is again distributional input about the order.

**10.3 Modelling assumptions.** Theorems 4.1–4.7 are stated for a cyclic group with a uniformly drawn point; Theorem 7.2 covers the rank-two case and Corollary 7.3 shows the cyclic model is conservative. The passage from "the group of points modulo the unknown prime" to "a cyclic group of order $m$ with $m$ drawn from some distribution" is the standard ECM modelling step and is not itself justified here.

---

## 11. Discussion

The empirical campaign posed a mechanism question — is low-bound stage-1 success collision luck or order completion firing early? — and answered it statistically. The arithmetic developed here answers it structurally, and in doing so explains why the statistical answer had to come out as it did.

The stage-1 success event is a divisibility (Theorem 3.2). Its count is a greatest common divisor (Theorem 4.1), identified as the powersmooth part of the order (Theorem 4.2). Its response to the smoothness budget is a monotone staircase (Theorem 5.1) that is constant between prime powers dividing the order (Theorem 5.2), jumps by an exactly known factor (Theorem 5.4), and saturates at powersmoothness (Theorem 5.3). Its position in the schedule is the largest prime factor of the order (Theorem 3.4), so the position distribution is supported on at most $\log_2 m$ of $\pi(B)$ steps (Theorem 4.6) and contains a flat block of length $\pi(B)/(\omega(m)+1)$ (Theorem 6.2). Where order completion is impossible, the rate is exactly $1/m$ (Theorem 7.1). And the folklore collision rate is dominated whenever the powersmooth part exceeds $1.44B$ (Theorem 7.5).

Every empirical signature is thereby accounted for: flatness in the dose (Theorem 5.2), stability across scales (Theorem 4.3), non-uniformity of firing position (Theorems 4.6 and 6.2), early firing (Theorem 4.7 and Corollary 3.5), the collision floor's subdominance (Theorems 7.1 and 7.5), and the observed multi-curve rates (Theorem 7.4). None of these required a probabilistic model of the success event; the only place randomness legitimately enters is the draw of the group order.

The practical reading stands: useful firing happens inside roughly the first $10$–$30\%$ of the schedule, and the remainder of stage 1 is, for a typical order, provably inert.

---

## 12. Future directions

**Distributional early fire from smooth-number analytics.** Combine Theorem 3.4 with quantitative estimates for the distribution of the largest prime factor of integers in a Hasse–Weil interval to obtain a genuine median statement. The right conditional shape is: for $m$ drawn from a distribution with a Dickman-type tail, $\mathbb{E}[\pi(\mathrm{lpf}(m))/\pi(B)]$ is small.

**From a flat run to a sup-distance bound.** Locate the inert block of Theorem 6.2 within the schedule and convert its length into an explicit lower bound on the Kolmogorov–Smirnov distance between the firing-position distribution and the uniform distribution on the schedule.

**Persistence where the smooth part must shrink.** The regime tested here keeps $B/p$ in a range where the powersmooth part remains substantial. The honest next question is whether early firing persists in the regime where $B/p$ must shrink — where the smoothness parameter $u = \log p/\log B$ grows into the $6$–$14$ range — since there Theorem 5.3's saturation is far from being reached and the staircase is genuinely partial.

**Stage-2 analogue.** Stage 2 of ECM tests one additional large prime beyond $B$. The corresponding exact event is $\mathrm{ord}(g) \mid k(B)\cdot q$ for a single prime $q$ in the stage-2 interval; the firing count becomes $\gcd(m, k(B)\,q)$, and the whole staircase theory should extend with an extra rank-one jump.

**Rank-two refinements.** Corollary 7.3 gives only an inequality. Quantifying the average gain of the true group structure over the cyclic model, as a function of the distribution of $(m_1,m_2)$, would sharpen predicted rates.

\begin{abstract}
Stage 1 of Lenstra's elliptic curve method (ECM) multiplies a starting point by the scalar
$k(B) = \prod_{q \le B} q^{\lfloor \log_q B\rfloor}$, accumulating one prime power at a time
along the schedule of primes $q \le B$. Folklore models the resulting success as a
\emph{collision}: a chance event of probability approximately $1 - e^{-1.44 B/p}$ per curve.
An empirical campaign at planted-prime bit lengths $26$ and $32$ found this model incompatible
with observation on two independent legs: success rates were flat in the smoothness budget
(three doses, rates $0.60$--$0.775$, all confidence intervals overlapping across scales), and
the position within the prime schedule at which successful runs fired was decisively
non-uniform, with medians in $[0.073, 0.293]$ and late-tail mass at most $13\%$.

We give a complete, unconditional arithmetic account of both phenomena, showing that no
probabilistic model of the \emph{event} is needed. We prove: (i) stage-1 firing on a point of
order $n$ is exactly the divisibility $n \mid k(B)$, equivalently $B$-powersmoothness of $n$;
(ii) in a cyclic group of order $m$ the number of firing points is exactly $\gcd(m, k(B))$,
the largest $B$-powersmooth divisor of $m$; (iii) the least schedule cutoff at which a firing
order fires is exactly its largest prime factor; (iv) the cumulative firing count is a
monotone staircase in the bound, constant unless the bound crosses a prime power dividing the
order, with exact multiplicative jump $q^{\min(v_q(m), \lfloor\log_q B\rfloor)}$, and maximal
precisely at powersmoothness; (v) the firing positions form a set of at most
$\omega(m) \le \log_2 m$ of the $\pi(B)$ schedule steps, hence cannot be uniform once the
schedule is long, and a pigeonhole argument produces an inert block of at least
$\pi(B)/(\omega(m)+1)$ schedule primes; (vi) with $c$ points the multi-curve success count is
exactly $m^c - (m-\gcd(m,k))^c$; (vii) where order completion is impossible the firing count
collapses to $1$, giving rate $1/m$; and (viii) any order-completion rate exceeding $1.44 B/m$
provably beats the collision baseline, since $1 - e^{-x} \le x$. A worked cell
($m = 720$, $B = 10$) exhibits the entire staircase, $1, 8, 72, 360, 360$, and a true rate of
$1/2$ against a collision ceiling of $1/50$.
\end{abstract}

\noindent\textbf{Keywords:} elliptic curve method, powersmooth, order completion, greatest

\section{Introduction}

\subsection{Setting}

Let $N$ be a composite integer with an unknown prime factor $p$. Lenstra's elliptic curve
method chooses a curve $E$ and a point $P$ over $\mathbb{Z}/N$ and computes $k\cdot P$ using
formulas requiring modular inversions. The method succeeds when an inversion fails modulo $p$
but not modulo $N$, which happens when the order of $P \bmod p$ in $E(\mathbb{F}_p)$ divides
$k$. Stage 1 uses the scalar
\[
k(B) \;=\; \prod_{\substack{q \le B\\ q\ \mathrm{prime}}} q^{\lfloor \log_q B\rfloor},
\]
built prime by prime in increasing order. We write $k(B,C)$ for the partial product over primes
$q \le C$, so $k(B,C)$ is the scalar accumulated after the schedule has processed all primes up
to $C$, and $k(B) = k(B,B)$.

\subsection{The two competing mechanisms}

Two stories are told about why a stage-1 run at a modest bound $B$ succeeds.

\emph{Order completion:} the order $n$ of the point genuinely divides $k(B)$.

\emph{Collision:} the success is a chance divisibility unrelated to smoothness of the order,
whose per-curve rate folklore puts at $1 - \exp(-1.44 B/p)$.

The two make different predictions. Collision predicts a \emph{dose response}: rates increasing
in $B$ and decaying as $p$ grows. It also predicts nothing in particular about \emph{when} in
the schedule a success occurs, so uniformity across the $\pi(B)$ steps is the natural null.
Order completion predicts flatness in $B$ across inert stretches, stability under increases of
scale that leave the smooth part alone, and heavily front-loaded firing positions.

\subsection{The empirical picture}

A pre-registered campaign, with a fresh random seed disjoint from earlier lineages, ran stage 1
only, with $40$ trials per bit length, three smoothness budgets ($\lceil 0.125\,T\rceil$,
$\lceil 0.5\,T\rceil$, $\lfloor 0.9\,T\rfloor$ of a target $T$), and three curves per trial. It
recorded:

\begin{itemize}
\item \textbf{Rate stability at every dose.} At bit length $26$: rates $0.65$, $0.75$, $0.60$;
at bit length $32$: $0.75$, $0.775$, $0.75$. Two-proportion tests gave $p = 0.329, 0.793,
0.152$; Wilson intervals overlapped at all three doses. No decay toward $1-\exp(-1.44B/p)$.
\item \textbf{Non-uniform, early firing.} Normalizing the schedule position of the successful
step to $[0,1]$, a goodness-of-fit test against the uniform distribution rejected in all six
cells ($p \le 0.002$); medians ranged over $[0.073, 0.293]$, and the mass in the top fifth of
the schedule never exceeded $13\%$.
\item \textbf{A separated collision floor.} Using the second, much larger prime factor $q$ of
the modulus as a control channel (for which $B \ll q$ makes order completion impossible), hits
at $q$ numbered $9$--$16$ per cell against $24$--$31$ at $p$. Independently, the first-curve
success rate at the smallest dose and largest scale was $0.425$, about $2.58$ times the
per-curve constant collision baseline $0.1647$.
\end{itemize}

We show that all three signatures are shadows of exact arithmetic facts.

\section{Definitions and notation}

Throughout, $q$ and $r$ denote primes, $v_r(n)$ the exponent of $r$ in $n$, $\omega(n)$ the
number of distinct prime factors of $n$, and $\pi(C)$ the number of primes $\le C$.

\begin{definition}[Truncated stage-1 scalar]
For $B, C \in \mathbb{N}$,
\[
k(B,C) \;=\; \prod_{\substack{q \le C \\ q\ \mathrm{prime}}} q^{\lfloor \log_q B\rfloor},
\qquad k(B) := k(B,B).
\]
Thus $k(B,C)$ is exactly the scalar stage 1 has accumulated after processing every schedule
prime up to $C$. Note $k(B,C)\ne 0$ and $k(B,C) \mid k(B,C')$ for $C \le C'$.
\end{definition}

\begin{definition}[Powersmoothness]
$n$ is \emph{$B$-powersmooth} if $q^{v_q(n)} \le B$ for every prime $q \mid n$.
\end{definition}

\begin{definition}[Firing set]
For $m > 0$ and a scalar $k$,
$F(m,k) = \{\, a \in \{0,\dots,m-1\} : m \mid k\,a \,\}$,
the residues of $\mathbb{Z}/m$ annihilated by multiplication by $k$. Modelling
$E(\mathbb{F}_p)$ as cyclic of order $m$ and the starting point as uniform, $|F(m,k)|/m$ is the
stage-1 success rate.
\end{definition}

\begin{definition}[Largest prime factor]
$\lpf(n) = \max\{q : q \mid n\}$, with $\lpf(1) = 0$.
\end{definition}

\begin{definition}[Schedule, jump set, large part]
The \emph{schedule} at bound $B$ is the set of primes $\le B$, of cardinality $\pi(B)$. The
\emph{jump set} $J(m,B)$ is the set of cutoffs $C \le B$ at which $C \mapsto \gcd(m, k(B,C))$
strictly increases. The \emph{large part} of $m$ above $L$ is
$\Lg(m,L) = \prod_{q \mid m,\ q > L} q^{v_q(m)}$.
\end{definition}

\begin{lemma}[Exponents of the scalar]\label{lem:exp}
For any prime $r$, $v_r(k(B,C)) = \lfloor \log_r B\rfloor$ if $r \le C$ and $0$ otherwise.
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}[Proof sketch]
The factorization of a product of prime powers over a set $S$ of distinct primes assigns to $r$
the exponent attached to $r$ if $r \in S$ and $0$ otherwise; here $S$ is the set of primes
$\le C$ and the exponent attached to $q$ is $\lfloor\log_q B\rfloor$.
\end{proof}

\section{The firing criterion and the firing cutoff}

\begin{theorem}[Truncated firing criterion]\label{thm:crit}
Let $n \ne 0$, $B \ne 0$. Then
$n \mid k(B,C)$ if and only if every prime $q \mid n$ satisfies $q \le C$ and
$q^{v_q(n)} \le B$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}[Proof sketch]
$n \mid k(B,C)$ iff $v_r(n) \le v_r(k(B,C))$ for all primes $r$. By Lemma~\ref{lem:exp} this
reads: for $r \le C$, $v_r(n) \le \lfloor\log_r B\rfloor$, which by the defining property of
the integer logarithm is exactly $r^{v_r(n)} \le B$; and for $r > C$, $v_r(n) \le 0$, i.e.
$r \nmid n$.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Order completion is exactly powersmoothness]\label{thm:oc}
For $n \ne 0$, $B \ne 0$: $n \mid k(B)$ iff $n$ is $B$-powersmooth. Consequently, for a group
element $g$ of finite order, $g^{\,k(B)} = 1$ iff $\ord(g)$ is $B$-powersmooth.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}[Proof sketch]
Apply Theorem~\ref{thm:crit} with $C = B$; the clause $q \le B$ is implied by
$q^{v_q(n)} \le B$ since $v_q(n)\ge 1$ forces $q \le q^{v_q(n)}$. The group form is
$\ord(g)\mid k(B) \iff g^{k(B)}=1$.
\end{proof}

\begin{remark}
This is the central conceptual point: the stage-1 success event contains no probabilistic
content whatsoever. Whatever randomness exists lives in the draw of the curve, i.e. in the
distribution of the group order, not in the event given that order.
\end{remark}

\begin{theorem}[No order completion above the bound]\label{thm:nooc}
If some prime power exactly dividing $\ord(g)$ exceeds $B$ --- in particular if $\ord(g)$ has
any prime factor $q > B$ --- then $g^{k(B)} \ne 1$, for every schedule.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}[Proof sketch]
Immediate from Theorem~\ref{thm:oc}: powersmoothness fails at that prime. For the prime-factor
form, $q \le q^{v_q}$.
\end{proof}

Theorem~\ref{thm:nooc} is the formal content of the experimental control channel: at the large
factor $q$ of the modulus with $B \ll q$, order completion is impossible, so hits there measure
the collision floor alone.

\begin{theorem}[The firing position is the largest prime factor]\label{thm:pos}
Let $n \ne 0$ be $B$-powersmooth. Then $n \mid k(B,C)$ iff $\lpf(n) \le C$; hence $\lpf(n)$ is
the least cutoff at which the accumulating scalar kills $n$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}[Proof sketch]
By Theorem~\ref{thm:crit}, powersmoothness already grants $q^{v_q(n)} \le B$ for all $q \mid
n$, so the criterion reduces to $q \le C$ for all $q \mid n$, i.e. $\lpf(n) \le C$.
\end{proof}

\begin{corollary}[Early fire, arithmetized]\label{cor:early}
If $n$ is $B$-powersmooth with $\lpf(n) \le L$, the run fires within the first $\pi(L)$ of its
$\pi(B)$ prime steps; the normalized firing position is at most $\pi(L)/\pi(B)$. Conversely, a
run that has not fired by cutoff $L$ has an order with a prime factor exceeding $L$.
\end{corollary}

\section{Exact counts and the greatest-common-divisor staircase}

\begin{theorem}[Exact firing count]\label{thm:count}
For $m > 0$ and any scalar $k$, $|F(m,k)| = \gcd(m,k)$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}[Proof sketch]
Write $g = \gcd(m,k)$, $d = m/g$. Since $m/g$ and $k/g$ are coprime, $m \mid k a \iff d \mid
a$. The multiples of $d$ below $m$ are $d\cdot 0,\dots,d\cdot(g-1)$, a set of size $g$ because
$j \mapsto dj$ is injective.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[The firing count is the powersmooth part]\label{thm:psp}
For $m \ne 0$, $B \ne 0$, the number $\gcd(m,k(B))$ divides $m$, is $B$-powersmooth, and is
divisible by every $B$-powersmooth divisor of $m$; it is the greatest $B$-powersmooth divisor
of $m$ in the divisibility order.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}[Proof sketch]
It divides $m$ and divides $k(B)$, so by Theorem~\ref{thm:oc} it is powersmooth. If $d \mid m$
is powersmooth then $d \mid k(B)$, hence $d \mid \gcd(m,k(B))$.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Scale invariance]\label{thm:scale}
If $w > 0$ is coprime to $k$, then $|F(mw,k)| = |F(m,k)|$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}[Proof sketch]
$\gcd(mw,k) = \gcd(m,k)$ when $\gcd(w,k)=1$.
\end{proof}

The part of the order above the smoothness bound is invisible to the mechanism: it dilutes the
\emph{rate} through the denominator but cannot alter the firing \emph{count}. This is the
arithmetic reason a scale increase leaving the smooth part statistically unchanged leaves the
mechanism unchanged, as observed between bit lengths $26$ and $32$.

\begin{theorem}[Flatness of the cumulative count]\label{thm:flat}
Let $m \ne 0$, $B \ne 0$, $C \le C'$. If no prime divisor of $m$ lies in $(C, C']$, then
$\gcd(m,k(B,C)) = \gcd(m,k(B,C'))$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}[Proof sketch]
One divisibility is monotonicity of $k(B,\cdot)$. For the other, apply Theorem~\ref{thm:crit}
to $n = \gcd(m,k(B,C'))$: each of its prime divisors divides $m$ and is $\le C'$, hence $\le C$
by hypothesis, so $n \mid k(B,C)$.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Exact description of the jump set]\label{thm:jump}
For $m \ne 0$, $B \ne 0$, $J(m,B) = \{\, q \text{ prime} : q \mid m,\ q \le B \,\}$, and hence
$|J(m,B)| \le \omega(m) \le \log_2 m$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}[Proof sketch]
Theorem~\ref{thm:flat} shows a jump can occur only at a prime divisor of $m$; conversely at
such a prime $q \le B$ the exponent of $q$ in the gcd rises from $0$ to
$\min(v_q(m),\lfloor \log_q B\rfloor) \ge 1$. The bound $\omega(m)\le\log_2 m$ holds since $m$
is at least the product of its distinct prime factors.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Sparsity and non-uniformity of firing positions]\label{thm:sparse}
The firing positions occupy at most a $\log_2 m / \pi(B)$ fraction of the schedule. If
$\log_2 m < \pi(B)$ there exists a schedule prime that is never a firing position, so the
distribution of firing positions is not uniform on the schedule.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}[Proof sketch]
Combine Theorem~\ref{thm:jump} with a cardinality count: if every schedule prime were a firing
position we would have $\pi(B) \le |J(m,B)| \le \log_2 m$.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Early fire, quantitative form]\label{thm:earlyq}
For $m \ne 0$ and $L \le B$,
\[
\gcd\bigl(m, k(B)\bigr) \;\Bigm|\; \gcd\bigl(m, k(B,L)\bigr)\cdot \Lg(m,L),
\qquad
\gcd\bigl(m,k(B)\bigr) \le \gcd\bigl(m, k(B,L)\bigr)\cdot \Lg(m,L).
\]
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}[Proof sketch]
Compare exponents prime by prime. For $r \le L$ both sides carry
$\min(v_r(m), \lfloor\log_r B\rfloor)$. For $r > L$ the right-hand side carries $v_r(m)$ from
the large part whenever $r \mid m$, which dominates $\min(v_r(m),\cdot)$.
\end{proof}

In words: everything that ever fires has already fired by cutoff $L$, up to the large-prime
part of the order.

\section{Dose response: a monotone staircase that saturates}

\begin{theorem}[Monotonicity in the bound]\label{thm:mono}
If $B \le B'$ then $k(B) \mid k(B')$, hence $\gcd(m,k(B)) \mid \gcd(m,k(B'))$ and
$\gcd(m,k(B)) \le \gcd(m,k(B'))$ for $m \ne 0$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}[Proof sketch]
Prime by prime: for $r \le B$ we have $r \le B'$ and
$\lfloor \log_r B\rfloor \le \lfloor\log_r B'\rfloor$; for $B < r \le B'$ the exponent rises
from $0$.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[No dose response]\label{thm:nodose}
Let $m, B, B' \ne 0$. If for every prime $q \mid m$ and every $1 \le j \le v_q(m)$ the
conditions $q^j \le B$ and $q^j \le B'$ are equivalent, then
$\gcd(m,k(B)) = \gcd(m,k(B'))$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}[Proof sketch]
Compare exponents. For $r \mid m$ the exponent of $r$ in $\gcd(m,k(B))$ is
$\min(v_r(m), \lfloor\log_r B\rfloor)$ if $r \le B$ and $0$ otherwise. The hypothesis at $j=1$
makes $r \le B$ and $r \le B'$ equivalent; and $\min(v,\lfloor\log_r B\rfloor)$ is the largest
$j \le v$ with $r^{j} \le B$, so the hypothesis for $1 \le j \le v_r(m)$ makes the two minima
equal. Primes not dividing $m$ contribute $0$ on both sides.
\end{proof}

Theorem~\ref{thm:nodose} is the exact statement matching the recorded flatness of success rates
in the budget fraction: rates are piecewise constant in the bound, with jumps only at the few
prime powers dividing the order.

\begin{theorem}[Saturation]\label{thm:sat}
For $m, B \ne 0$: $\gcd(m,k(B)) = m$ if and only if $m$ is $B$-powersmooth.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}[Proof sketch]
$\gcd(m,k(B)) = m \iff m \mid k(B) \iff$ powersmoothness, by Theorem~\ref{thm:oc}.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Exact jump formula]\label{thm:jumpf}
For $m \ne 0$ and $q$ prime,
\[
\gcd\bigl(m, k(B,q)\bigr) \;=\; \gcd\bigl(m, k(B,q-1)\bigr)\cdot
q^{\min\left(v_q(m),\, \lfloor \log_q B\rfloor\right)} .
\]
In particular the count is unchanged when $q \nmid m$ or when $q > B$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}[Proof sketch]
Compare exponents at each prime $r$. At $r = q$ the left side carries
$\min(v_q(m), \lfloor \log_q B\rfloor)$ and the right side $0$ plus the same quantity. At
$r \ne q$ the conditions $r \le q$ and $r \le q-1$ agree and the extra factor contributes $0$.
\end{proof}

\section{The long inert block: a pigeonhole obstruction to uniformity}

\begin{lemma}[Same jump count implies same firing count]\label{lem:samecount}
For $C \le C' \le B$, if the number of jump primes $\le C$ equals the number of jump primes
$\le C'$, then $\gcd(m,k(B,C)) = \gcd(m,k(B,C'))$.
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}[Proof sketch]
The two filtered sets are nested with equal cardinality, hence equal; so no prime divisor of
$m$ lies in $(C,C']$, and Theorem~\ref{thm:flat} applies.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Existence of a long inert block]\label{thm:inert}
For $m, B \ne 0$ there is a set $S$ of schedule primes with
$|S| \ge \pi(B)/(\omega(m)+1)$
on which the firing count is constant.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}[Proof sketch]
Map each schedule prime $C$ to the number of jump primes $\le C$, a value in
$\{0,\dots,\omega(m)\}$ by Theorem~\ref{thm:jump}. The schedule has $\pi(B)$ elements and the
target $\omega(m)+1$ values, so some fiber has size at least $\pi(B)/(\omega(m)+1)$;
Lemma~\ref{lem:samecount} makes the count constant on any fiber.
\end{proof}

\begin{corollary}
If $\omega(m) \le 1$, at least half of the schedule is inert.
\end{corollary}

The uniform comparison distribution increases at every one of the $\pi(B)$ steps; a block of
that length on which the cumulative count is exactly constant is precisely the feature a
Kolmogorov--Smirnov-type statistic responds to.

\section{Controls, amplification, and the collision baseline}

\begin{theorem}[Collapse when order completion is impossible]\label{thm:control}
If every prime factor of $m$ exceeds $B$, then $\gcd(m,k(B)) = 1$: only the identity fires, and
the order-completion rate is exactly $1/m$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}[Proof sketch]
By Theorem~\ref{thm:psp} the gcd is a powersmooth divisor of $m$; a prime factor $q$ of it
would satisfy $q \mid m$ and $q \le q^{v_q} \le B$, contradicting the hypothesis.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Firing count in a rank-two group]\label{thm:rank2}
The number of points of $\mathbb{Z}/m_1\times\mathbb{Z}/m_2$ annihilated by $k$ is
$\gcd(m_1,k)\cdot\gcd(m_2,k)$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}[Proof sketch]
The firing set is the product $F(m_1,k)\times F(m_2,k)$; apply Theorem~\ref{thm:count} to each
factor.
\end{proof}

\begin{corollary}[Rank two fires at least as often]
$\gcd(m_1 m_2, k) \le \gcd(m_1,k)\cdot\gcd(m_2,k)$.
\end{corollary}

\begin{theorem}[Exact multi-curve count]\label{thm:multi}
With $c$ independently chosen points of a cyclic group of order $m$, the number of $c$-tuples
on which stage 1 fires at least once is exactly $m^{c} - (m - \gcd(m,k))^{c}$, so the success
rate is exactly $1 - (1-\rho)^{c}$ with $\rho = \gcd(m,k)/m$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}[Proof sketch]
The complementary event ``no coordinate fires'' is a product set: each coordinate ranges over
the $m - \gcd(m,k)$ non-firing residues. Subtract from $m^c$.
\end{proof}

No independence \emph{assumption} is made: this is a count of tuples in a product set.

\begin{theorem}[Order completion beats the baseline]\label{thm:beats}
For $m > 0$, if $\gcd(m, k(B)) > 1.44\,B$, then
\[
1 - \exp\!\left(-\frac{1.44\,B}{m}\right) \;<\; \frac{\gcd(m,k(B))}{m}.
\]
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}[Proof sketch]
$1 - e^{-x}\le x$ for all real $x$ (from $1 + t \le e^{t}$ at $t = -x$), so the baseline is at
most $1.44 B/m$; the hypothesis gives $1.44 B/m < \gcd(m,k(B))/m$.
\end{proof}

\section{A fully worked cell: \texorpdfstring{$m = 720$, $B = 10$}{m = 720, B = 10}}

Take $m = 720 = 2^4\cdot 3^2\cdot 5$ and $B = 10$. Then
$k(10) = 2^{3}\cdot 3^{2}\cdot 5\cdot 7 = 2520$ and $\gcd(720, 2520) = 360$.

\paragraph{The exact rate.} By Theorem~\ref{thm:count}, exactly $360$ of the $720$ residues
fire: rate $1/2$. By Theorem~\ref{thm:psp}, $360 = 2^3\cdot3^2\cdot5$ is the largest
$10$-powersmooth divisor of $720$; the factor $2^4 = 16 > 10$ is exactly what is lost.

\paragraph{The staircase.} Advancing the cutoff through $1, 2, 3, 5, 7, 10$, the cumulative
firing counts $\gcd(720, k(10,C))$ are
\[
1,\quad 8,\quad 72,\quad 360,\quad 360,\quad 360 .
\]
Each step matches Theorem~\ref{thm:jumpf}: $2^{\min(4,3)} = 8$, then $\times 3^{\min(2,2)}=9$,
then $\times 5^{\min(1,1)}=5$, then $\times 7^{\min(0,1)}=1$. Two of the four schedule primes do
nothing.

\paragraph{Early fire.} $5\cdot\gcd(720, k(10,3)) = 5\cdot 72 = 360 = \gcd(720,k(10,10))$ and
$2\cdot 360 = 720$: half of the whole group fires, and one fifth of all points that ever fire
have already fired after the first two of the four schedule primes.

\paragraph{Against the collision baseline.} The heuristic per-curve collision rate is at most
$1.44\cdot 10/720 = 0.02$, while the true order-completion rate is $0.5$ --- more than $25$
times larger; Theorem~\ref{thm:beats} applies since $360 > 14.4$.

\paragraph{Multi-curve.} With $c = 3$, Theorem~\ref{thm:multi} gives exactly $720^3 - 360^3$
successful triples, a rate of $1 - (1/2)^3 = 7/8$.

\section{Algorithmic consequences}

\paragraph{Schedule pruning is bounded by the jump set.} By Theorem~\ref{thm:jump} only the
primes dividing the group order can change the firing count: at most $\omega(m) \le \log_2 m$
of the $\pi(B)$ steps matter, and by Theorem~\ref{thm:pos} the last of them is $\lpf(m)$.

\paragraph{Budget allocation should be front-loaded.} Theorem~\ref{thm:earlyq} says everything
but the large-prime part has already fired by any cutoff $L$. Under a fixed budget, more curves
at a modest bound beat fewer curves at a large bound exactly when the staircase for a typical
order has already saturated below the modest bound; Theorem~\ref{thm:multi} quantifies the
trade.

\paragraph{Dose response is not a tuning signal.} Theorem~\ref{thm:nodose} says zero rate change
is the \emph{predicted} outcome unless the increase crosses a prime power dividing the order.
Absence of dose response is evidence \emph{for} order completion.

\paragraph{Computational kernels.} Given $m$ and $B$, the staircase $C \mapsto \gcd(m,k(B,C))$
is computed by sieving primes up to $B$ ($O(B\log\log B)$) and applying the update of
Theorem~\ref{thm:jumpf}, for $O(\pi(B)\log m)$ arithmetic operations, never forming the
astronomically large scalar $k(B)$. Deciding firing and locating the position requires
factoring $m$, testing $q^{v_q(m)} \le B$ for all $q \mid m$, and returning
$\pi(\lpf(m))/\pi(B)$; correctness is Theorems~\ref{thm:oc} and~\ref{thm:pos}.

\section{Limitations}

\paragraph{A distributional early-fire theorem.} ``The median normalized firing position is at
most $0.3$'' cannot be proved from arithmetic alone. For a single order the position is
deterministic ($\pi(\lpf(m))/\pi(B)$), so a median statement concerns a family, i.e. the
distribution of largest prime factors of powersmooth numbers --- Dickman-type analytic input.
What survives unconditionally is Theorem~\ref{thm:earlyq}.

\paragraph{A quantitative distance-to-uniform bound.} We prove the support-size version
(Theorem~\ref{thm:sparse}) and the long-inert-block version (Theorem~\ref{thm:inert}), which
together make uniformity impossible. Converting a flat block of length $\ell$ into a lower
bound on the Kolmogorov--Smirnov distance requires locating the block: a run at the boundary
contributes little sup-distance, a run straddling the middle about $\ell/(2\pi(B))$.

\paragraph{Modelling assumptions.} The counts are stated for a cyclic group with a uniformly
drawn point; Theorem~\ref{thm:rank2} covers rank two and shows the cyclic model is
conservative. The passage from the true group of points to a random cyclic order is the
standard ECM modelling step and is not justified here.

\section{Discussion}

The stage-1 success event is a divisibility (Theorem~\ref{thm:oc}). Its count is a greatest
common divisor (Theorem~\ref{thm:count}), identified as the powersmooth part of the order
(Theorem~\ref{thm:psp}). Its response to the budget is a monotone staircase
(Theorem~\ref{thm:mono}) that is constant between prime powers dividing the order
(Theorem~\ref{thm:nodose}), jumps by an exactly known factor (Theorem~\ref{thm:jumpf}) and
saturates at powersmoothness (Theorem~\ref{thm:sat}). Its position is the largest prime factor
(Theorem~\ref{thm:pos}), so the position distribution is supported on at most $\log_2 m$ of
$\pi(B)$ steps (Theorem~\ref{thm:sparse}) and contains a flat block of length
$\pi(B)/(\omega(m)+1)$ (Theorem~\ref{thm:inert}). Where order completion is impossible the rate
is exactly $1/m$ (Theorem~\ref{thm:control}), and the folklore collision rate is dominated
whenever the powersmooth part exceeds $1.44B$ (Theorem~\ref{thm:beats}).

Every empirical signature is thereby accounted for: flatness in dose, stability across scales,
non-uniformity of firing position, early firing, subdominance of the collision floor, and the
observed multi-curve rates. None required a probabilistic model of the success event; the only
place randomness legitimately enters is the draw of the group order.

\section{Future directions}

\begin{itemize}
\item \textbf{Distributional early fire.} Combine Theorem~\ref{thm:pos} with quantitative
estimates for the distribution of the largest prime factor of integers in a Hasse--Weil
interval to obtain a genuine median statement.
\item \textbf{From a flat run to a sup-distance bound.} Locate the inert block of
Theorem~\ref{thm:inert} within the schedule and convert its length into an explicit lower bound
on the distance to uniformity.
\item \textbf{Persistence where the smooth part must shrink.} Test whether early firing
persists where $B/p$ must shrink, i.e. where $u = \log p/\log B$ grows into the $6$--$14$
range and saturation is far from reached.
\item \textbf{Stage-2 analogue.} Stage 2 tests one additional large prime $q$ beyond $B$; the
exact event is $\ord(g) \mid k(B)\,q$ and the count becomes $\gcd(m, k(B) q)$, so the staircase
theory should extend with an extra rank-one jump.
\item \textbf{Rank-two refinements.} Quantify the average gain of the true group structure over
the cyclic model as a function of the distribution of $(m_1,m_2)$.
\end{itemize}

from __future__ import annotations

import math
import random
from collections import Counter
from math import gcd
from typing import Dict, List, Tuple

# ----------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Basic arithmetic utilities
# ----------------------------------------------------------------------------


def primes_up_to(n: int) -> List[int]:
    """All primes <= n by a sieve of Eratosthenes.  Cost O(n log log n)."""
    if n < 2:
        return []
    sieve = bytearray([1]) * (n + 1)
    sieve[0] = sieve[1] = 0
    for p in range(2, int(n**0.5) + 1):
        if sieve[p]:
            sieve[p * p :: p] = bytearray(len(sieve[p * p :: p]))
    return [i for i in range(n + 1) if sieve[i]]


def factorize(n: int) -> Dict[int, int]:
    """Prime factorization of n >= 1 as {prime: exponent} by trial division."""
    assert n >= 1
    factors: Dict[int, int] = {}
    d = 2
    while d * d <= n:
        while n % d == 0:
            factors[d] = factors.get(d, 0) + 1
            n //= d
        d += 1 if d == 2 else 2
    if n > 1:
        factors[n] = factors.get(n, 0) + 1
    return factors


def integer_log(base: int, x: int) -> int:
    """floor(log_base x) for base >= 2, x >= 1, computed exactly in integers."""
    assert base >= 2 and x >= 1
    e, p = 0, 1
    while p * base <= x:
        p *= base
        e += 1
    return e


def stage1_scalar(bound: int, cutoff: int | None = None) -> int:
    """k(B, C) = prod over primes q <= C of q^floor(log_q B).  Default C = B."""
    if cutoff is None:
        cutoff = bound
    k = 1
    for q in primes_up_to(min(cutoff, bound)):
        k *= q ** integer_log(q, bound)
    return k


def is_powersmooth(bound: int, n: int) -> bool:
    """n is B-powersmooth: every prime power exactly dividing n is <= B."""
    return all(q**v <= bound for q, v in factorize(n).items())


def largest_prime_factor(n: int) -> int:
    """lpf(n); by convention 0 for n = 1."""
    f = factorize(n)
    return max(f) if f else 0


def large_part(m: int, cutoff: int) -> int:
    """The part of m supported on primes > cutoff."""
    out = 1
    for q, v in factorize(m).items():
        if q > cutoff:
            out *= q**v
    return out


# ----------------------------------------------------------------------------
# The exact objects of the theory
# ----------------------------------------------------------------------------


def firing_set(m: int, k: int) -> List[int]:
    """{a in Z/m : m | k a}.  Brute force; used only to CHECK the gcd formula."""
    return [a for a in range(m) if (k * a) % m == 0]


def firing_count(m: int, k: int) -> int:
    """Theorem: the number of firing residues is exactly gcd(m, k)."""
    return gcd(m, k)


def powersmooth_part(m: int, bound: int) -> int:
    """Directly the greatest B-powersmooth divisor of m, from the factorization."""
    out = 1
    for q, v in factorize(m).items():
        j = min(v, integer_log(q, bound))
        out *= q**j
    return out


def staircase(m: int, bound: int) -> List[Tuple[int, int]]:
    """
    The cumulative firing counts (q, gcd(m, k(B,q))) as q runs over the schedule.

    Uses the exact jump formula (multiply by q^min(v_q(m), floor(log_q B)))
    rather than forming the astronomically large scalar k(B).
    Cost: O(pi(B) log m) big-integer multiplications.
    """
    fm = factorize(m)
    count = 1
    out: List[Tuple[int, int]] = []
    for q in primes_up_to(bound):
        count *= q ** min(fm.get(q, 0), integer_log(q, bound))
        out.append((q, count))
    return out


def jump_set(m: int, bound: int) -> List[int]:
    """Schedule primes at which the count strictly increases = {q | m, q <= B}."""
    return [q for q in factorize(m) if q <= bound]


def firing_cutoff(m: int, bound: int) -> int | None:
    """Least schedule cutoff at which a B-powersmooth order fires; None if it never does."""
    if not is_powersmooth(bound, m):
        return None
    return largest_prime_factor(m)


def normalized_firing_position(m: int, bound: int) -> float | None:
    """pi(lpf(m)) / pi(B): where in the schedule the run fires, rescaled to [0,1]."""
    c = firing_cutoff(m, bound)
    if c is None:
        return None
    sched = primes_up_to(bound)
    if not sched:
        return None
    return sum(1 for q in sched if q <= c) / len(sched)


def multi_curve_success_count(m: int, k: int, curves: int) -> int:
    """Exactly m^c - (m - gcd(m,k))^c tuples on which stage 1 fires at least once."""
    return m**curves - (m - gcd(m, k)) ** curves


def collision_baseline(bound: int, m: int) -> float:
    """The folklore per-curve collision rate 1 - exp(-1.44 B / m)."""
    return 1.0 - math.exp(-1.44 * bound / m)


def longest_inert_block(m: int, bound: int) -> int:
    """Largest number of schedule primes sharing one and the same firing count."""
    counts = Counter(c for _, c in staircase(m, bound))
    return max(counts.values()) if counts else 0

def demo_firing_criterion() -> None:
    """Check n | k(B) <=> n is B-powersmooth, and the position theorem."""

    """

    target, three smoothness budgets, three curves.  Reports success rates and
    the distribution of normalized firing positions, all computed EXACTLY from
    the theory rather than by simulating curve arithmetic.

    banner("10.  Simulated campaign: flat rates and early, non-uniform firing")
    rng = random.Random(20260903)
    trials = 300
    curves = 3
    target = 20000  # the bound target T; budgets are fractions of it
    print(f"  {trials} random orders m near 2^20, {curves} curves, budgets"
          f" 0.125T, 0.5T, 0.9T with T = {target}")
    print()
    print("   budget    B    success rate   median firing position   tail(>=0.8)")
    orders = [rng.randrange(2**19, 2**20) for _ in range(trials)]
    for frac in (0.125, 0.5, 0.9):
        B = max(2, int(frac * target))
        successes = 0
        positions: List[float] = []
        for m in orders:
            rho = powersmooth_part(m, B) / m
            # exact c-curve success probability for this order
            p = 1 - (1 - rho) ** curves
            if rng.random() < p:
                successes += 1

                if pos is not None:

        med = positions[len(positions) // 2] if positions else float("nan")
        tail = sum(1 for p in positions if p >= 0.8) / max(1, len(positions))
        print(f"   {frac:>5}   {B:>4}      {successes/trials:.3f}"
              f"                 {med:.3f}              {tail:.3f}")
    print()
    print("  A 7-fold increase of the budget moves the success rate by well under a")
    print("  factor of two -- the staircase is already largely climbed -- while the")
    print("  firing positions sit far below 0.5 with a thin upper tail, and the shape")
    print("  deepens with the dose.  Both signatures are consequences of the exact")

from __future__ import annotations

import math
import random
from collections import Counter
from math import gcd
from typing import Dict, List, Tuple

# ----------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Basic arithmetic utilities
# ----------------------------------------------------------------------------


def primes_up_to(n: int) -> List[int]:
    """All primes <= n by a sieve of Eratosthenes.  Cost O(n log log n)."""
    if n < 2:
        return []
    sieve = bytearray([1]) * (n + 1)
    sieve[0] = sieve[1] = 0
    for p in range(2, int(n**0.5) + 1):
        if sieve[p]:
            sieve[p * p :: p] = bytearray(len(sieve[p * p :: p]))
    return [i for i in range(n + 1) if sieve[i]]


def factorize(n: int) -> Dict[int, int]:
    """Prime factorization of n >= 1 as {prime: exponent} by trial division."""
    assert n >= 1
    factors: Dict[int, int] = {}
    d = 2
    while d * d <= n:
        while n % d == 0:
            factors[d] = factors.get(d, 0) + 1
            n //= d
        d += 1 if d == 2 else 2
    if n > 1:
        factors[n] = factors.get(n, 0) + 1
    return factors


def integer_log(base: int, x: int) -> int:
    """floor(log_base x) for base >= 2, x >= 1, computed exactly in integers."""
    assert base >= 2 and x >= 1
    e, p = 0, 1
    while p * base <= x:
        p *= base
        e += 1
    return e


def stage1_scalar(bound: int, cutoff: int | None = None) -> int:
    """k(B, C) = prod over primes q <= C of q^floor(log_q B).  Default C = B."""
    if cutoff is None:
        cutoff = bound
    k = 1
    for q in primes_up_to(min(cutoff, bound)):
        k *= q ** integer_log(q, bound)
    return k


def is_powersmooth(bound: int, n: int) -> bool:
    """n is B-powersmooth: every prime power exactly dividing n is <= B."""
    return all(q**v <= bound for q, v in factorize(n).items())


def largest_prime_factor(n: int) -> int:
    """lpf(n); by convention 0 for n = 1."""
    f = factorize(n)
    return max(f) if f else 0


def large_part(m: int, cutoff: int) -> int:
    """The part of m supported on primes > cutoff."""
    out = 1
    for q, v in factorize(m).items():
        if q > cutoff:
            out *= q**v
    return out


# ----------------------------------------------------------------------------
# The exact objects of the theory
# ----------------------------------------------------------------------------


def firing_set(m: int, k: int) -> List[int]:
    """{a in Z/m : m | k a}.  Brute force; used only to CHECK the gcd formula."""
    return [a for a in range(m) if (k * a) % m == 0]


def firing_count(m: int, k: int) -> int:
    """Theorem: the number of firing residues is exactly gcd(m, k)."""
    return gcd(m, k)


def powersmooth_part(m: int, bound: int) -> int:
    """Directly the greatest B-powersmooth divisor of m, from the factorization."""
    out = 1
    for q, v in factorize(m).items():
        j = min(v, integer_log(q, bound))
        out *= q**j
    return out


def staircase(m: int, bound: int) -> List[Tuple[int, int]]:
    """
    The cumulative firing counts (q, gcd(m, k(B,q))) as q runs over the schedule.

    Uses the exact jump formula (multiply by q^min(v_q(m), floor(log_q B)))
    rather than forming the astronomically large scalar k(B).
    Cost: O(pi(B) log m) big-integer multiplications.
    """
    fm = factorize(m)
    count = 1
    out: List[Tuple[int, int]] = []
    for q in primes_up_to(bound):
        count *= q ** min(fm.get(q, 0), integer_log(q, bound))
        out.append((q, count))
    return out


def jump_set(m: int, bound: int) -> List[int]:
    """Schedule primes at which the count strictly increases = {q | m, q <= B}."""
    return [q for q in factorize(m) if q <= bound]


def firing_cutoff(m: int, bound: int) -> int | None:
    """Least schedule cutoff at which a B-powersmooth order fires; None if it never does."""
    if not is_powersmooth(bound, m):
        return None
    return largest_prime_factor(m)


def normalized_firing_position(m: int, bound: int) -> float | None:
    """pi(lpf(m)) / pi(B): where in the schedule the run fires, rescaled to [0,1]."""
    c = firing_cutoff(m, bound)
    if c is None:
        return None
    sched = primes_up_to(bound)
    if not sched:
        return None
    return sum(1 for q in sched if q <= c) / len(sched)


def multi_curve_success_count(m: int, k: int, curves: int) -> int:
    """Exactly m^c - (m - gcd(m,k))^c tuples on which stage 1 fires at least once."""
    return m**curves - (m - gcd(m, k)) ** curves


def collision_baseline(bound: int, m: int) -> float:
    """The folklore per-curve collision rate 1 - exp(-1.44 B / m)."""
    return 1.0 - math.exp(-1.44 * bound / m)


def longest_inert_block(m: int, bound: int) -> int:
    """Largest number of schedule primes sharing one and the same firing count."""
    counts = Counter(c for _, c in staircase(m, bound))
    return max(counts.values()) if counts else 0

def factorize(n: int) -> Dict[int, int]:
    """Prime factorization by trial division."""
    factors: Dict[int, int] = {}
    d = 2
    while d * d <= n:
        while n % d == 0:
            factors[d] = factors.get(d, 0) + 1
            n //= d
        d += 1 if d == 2 else 2
    if n > 1:
        factors[n] = factors.get(n, 0) + 1
    return factors


def integer_log(base: int, x: int) -> int:
    e, p = 0, 1
    while p * base <= x:
        p *= base
        e += 1
    return e


def powersmooth_part(m: int, bound: int) -> int:
    """The greatest B-powersmooth divisor of m; equals gcd(m, k(B))."""
    out = 1
    for q, v in factorize(m).items():
        out *= q ** min(v, integer_log(q, bound))
    return out


def multi_curve_rate(m: int, bound: int, curves: int) -> float:
    """Exact c-curve success rate 1 - (1 - rho)^c with rho = gcd(m,k(B))/m."""
    rho = powersmooth_part(m, bound) / m
    return 1.0 - (1.0 - rho) ** curves


def mean_and_ci(values: List[float]) -> Tuple[float, float, float]:
    """Sample mean and a 95% normal confidence interval."""
    n = len(values)
    mu = sum(values) / n
    var = sum((v - mu) ** 2 for v in values) / max(1, n - 1)
    half = 1.96 * math.sqrt(var / n)
    return mu, max(0.0, mu - half), min(1.0, mu + half)


def sample_orders(rng: random.Random, bits: int, count: int) -> List[int]:
    """Random group orders in the Hasse interval around a prime of `bits` bits."""
    return [rng.randrange(2 ** (bits - 1), 2**bits) for _ in range(count)]


def all_factors_above(m: int, bound: int) -> bool:
    return all(q > bound for q in factorize(m))

from __future__ import annotations

from math import gcd
from typing import Dict, List, Tuple


def primes_up_to(n: int) -> List[int]:
    """Sieve of Eratosthenes; cost O(n log log n)."""
    if n < 2:
        return []
    sieve = bytearray([1]) * (n + 1)
    sieve[0] = sieve[1] = 0
    for p in range(2, int(n**0.5) + 1):
        if sieve[p]:
            sieve[p * p :: p] = bytearray(len(sieve[p * p :: p]))
    return [i for i in range(n + 1) if sieve[i]]


def factorize(n: int) -> Dict[int, int]:
    """Prime factorization by trial division; cost O(sqrt n)."""
    factors: Dict[int, int] = {}
    d = 2
    while d * d <= n:
        while n % d == 0:
            factors[d] = factors.get(d, 0) + 1
            n //= d
        d += 1 if d == 2 else 2
    if n > 1:
        factors[n] = factors.get(n, 0) + 1
    return factors


def integer_log(base: int, x: int) -> int:
    """floor(log_base x), exactly, in integer arithmetic."""
    e, p = 0, 1
    while p * base <= x:
        p *= base
        e += 1
    return e


def firing_staircase(m: int, bound: int) -> List[Tuple[int, int, int]]:
    """
    Return [(q, jump factor at q, cumulative firing count after q)] for every
    prime q of the schedule at smoothness bound `bound`.

    The cumulative count after cutoff C equals gcd(m, k(B,C)); it is built here
    by the exact jump formula, multiplying by q^min(v_q(m), floor(log_q B)) as
    each schedule prime is passed, so the astronomically large scalar k(B) is
    never formed.
    """
    fm = factorize(m)
    count = 1
    rows: List[Tuple[int, int, int]] = []
    for q in primes_up_to(bound):
        gain = q ** min(fm.get(q, 0), integer_log(q, bound))
        count *= gain
        rows.append((q, gain, count))
    return rows


def firing_rate(m: int, bound: int) -> float:
    """The exact one-curve stage-1 success rate gcd(m, k(B)) / m."""
    rows = firing_staircase(m, bound)
    total = rows[-1][2] if rows else 1
    return total / m

    return factors


def is_powersmooth(bound: int, n: int) -> bool:
    """n is B-powersmooth iff every prime power exactly dividing n is <= B."""
    return all(q**v <= bound for q, v in factorize(n).items())


def firing_report(order: int, bound: int) -> Tuple[bool, Optional[int], Optional[float]]:
    """
    Decide whether stage 1 at bound `bound` fires on a point of the given order,
    and if so return the exact schedule cutoff at which it fires together with
    the normalized position of that cutoff in the schedule.

    Correctness: firing is equivalent to B-powersmoothness of the order, and the
    least firing cutoff is exactly the largest prime factor of the order.
    Cost: one factorization plus one sieve, O(sqrt(order) + B log log B).
    """
    f = factorize(order)
    if not all(q**v <= bound for q, v in f.items()):
        return (False, None, None)
    if not f:  # order 1: fires immediately
        return (True, 0, 0.0)
    cutoff = max(f)
    schedule = primes_up_to(bound)
    position = sum(1 for q in schedule if q <= cutoff) / len(schedule)
    return (True, cutoff, position)

from __future__ import annotations

from collections import Counter
from typing import Dict, List, Tuple


def primes_up_to(n: int) -> List[int]:
    if n < 2:
        return []
    sieve = bytearray([1]) * (n + 1)
    sieve[0] = sieve[1] = 0
    for p in range(2, int(n**0.5) + 1):
        if sieve[p]:
            sieve[p * p :: p] = bytearray(len(sieve[p * p :: p]))
    return [i for i in range(n + 1) if sieve[i]]


def factorize(n: int) -> Dict[int, int]:
    factors: Dict[int, int] = {}
    d = 2
    while d * d <= n:
        while n % d == 0:
            factors[d] = factors.get(d, 0) + 1
            n //= d
        d += 1 if d == 2 else 2
    if n > 1:
        factors[n] = factors.get(n, 0) + 1
    return factors


def inert_block(m: int, bound: int) -> Tuple[List[int], int, float]:
    """
    Return (the longest maximal block of schedule primes on which the firing
    count is constant, its length, the pigeonhole guarantee pi(B)/(omega(m)+1)).

    The firing count changes only at the primes dividing m, of which there are
    at most omega(m); mapping each schedule prime to the number of jump primes
    below it and applying the pigeonhole principle to the pi(B) schedule primes
    gives a fiber of size at least pi(B)/(omega(m)+1) on which the count is
    constant.  Cost: O(B log log B + sqrt m).
    """
    schedule = primes_up_to(bound)
    jump_primes = {q for q in factorize(m) if q <= bound}
    labels: List[int] = []
    seen = 0
    for q in schedule:
        if q in jump_primes:
            seen += 1
        labels.append(seen)
    counts = Counter(labels)
    best_label, best_len = counts.most_common(1)[0]
    block = [q for q, lab in zip(schedule, labels) if lab == best_label]
    guarantee = len(schedule) / (len(factorize(m)) + 1)
    return block, best_len, guarantee

from math import exp, log
from typing import Dict, List, Tuple

import matplotlib.pyplot as plt


def primes_up_to(n: int) -> List[int]:
    if n < 2:

    sieve = bytearray([1]) * (n + 1)
    sieve[0] = sieve[1] = 0
    for p in range(2, int(n**0.5) + 1):
        if sieve[p]:
            sieve[p * p :: p] = bytearray(len(sieve[p * p :: p]))
    return [i for i in range(n + 1) if sieve[i]]


def factorize(n: int) -> Dict[int, int]:
    factors: Dict[int, int] = {}
    d = 2
    while d * d <= n:
        while n % d == 0:
            factors[d] = factors.get(d, 0) + 1
            n //= d
        d += 1 if d == 2 else 2
    if n > 1:
        factors[n] = factors.get(n, 0) + 1
    return factors


def integer_log(base: int, x: int) -> int:
    e, p = 0, 1
    while p * base <= x:
        p *= base
        e += 1
    return e


def powersmooth_part(m: int, bound: int) -> int:
    out = 1
    for q, v in factorize(m).items():
        out *= q ** min(v, integer_log(q, bound))
    return out


def staircase(m: int, bound: int) -> List[Tuple[int, int, int]]:
    """(prime, jump factor, cumulative count) for every schedule prime."""
    fm = factorize(m)
    count = 1
    rows: List[Tuple[int, int, int]] = []
    for q in primes_up_to(bound):
        gain = q ** min(fm.get(q, 0), integer_log(q, bound))
        count *= gain
        rows.append((q, gain, count))
    return rows

"use strict";

function primesUpTo(n){
  if(n < 2) return [];
  const s = new Uint8Array(n+1).fill(1); s[0]=0; s[1]=0;
  for(let p=2;p*p<=n;p++) if(s[p]) for(let q=p*p;q<=n;q+=p) s[q]=0;
  const out=[]; for(let i=2;i<=n;i++) if(s[i]) out.push(i); return out;
}
function factorize(n){
  const f={}; let d=2;
  while(d*d<=n){ while(n%d===0){ f[d]=(f[d]||0)+1; n/=d; } d += (d===2?1:2); }
  if(n>1) f[n]=(f[n]||0)+1; return f;
}
function ilog(base,x){ let e=0,p=1; while(p*base<=x){ p*=base; e++; } return e; }
function smoothPart(m,B){
  const f=factorize(m); let out=1;
  for(const q in f){ const qq=+q; out *= Math.pow(qq, Math.min(f[q], ilog(qq,B))); }
  return out;
}
function lpf(n){ const f=factorize(n); const ks=Object.keys(f).map(Number); return ks.length?Math.max(...ks):0; }

function compute(){

  const B = Math.max(2, Math.round(+document.getElementById('bBox').value));
  const c = +document.getElementById('cSlide').value;
  const sched = primesUpTo(B);
  const f = factorize(m);
  let run = 1;
  const steps = sched.map(q=>{
    const j = Math.min(f[q]||0, ilog(q,B));
    const gain = Math.pow(q, j);
    run *= gain;
    return {q:q, gain:gain, count:run, jump: gain>1};
  });
  const g = smoothPart(m,B);
  return {m:m,B:B,c:c,sched:sched,f:f,steps:steps,g:g};
}

function fmtPct(x){ return (100*x).toFixed(x<0.001?4:2)+'%'; }

  const {m,B,c,sched,f,steps,g} = S;

  // ---- summary panel ----

      .map(q=> f[q]===1? q : q+'<sup>'+f[q]+'</sup>').join(' · ');

  } else {
    v.className='verdict bad';
    v.innerHTML = '<b>Order completion is negligible here.</b> The smooth part of the order is tiny, so '+
      'the whole success budget would have to come from chance collisions — exactly the control regime.';

  // ---- staircase ----

  const W=cv.width,H=cv.height,padL=62,padR=18,padT=18,padB=34;
  ctx.clearRect(0,0,W,H);
  const n = steps.length;
  const yMax = Math.log(Math.max(m, g))+0.6;
  const X = i => padL + (n<=1?0:(W-padL-padR)*i/(n-1));
  const Y = val => H-padB - (H-padT-padB)*Math.log(Math.max(1,val))/yMax;

  ctx.fillText('schedule primes  2 … '+B, W/2-70, H-8);

  const DW=dv.width,DH=dv.height,dL=62,dR=18,dT=16,dB=34;
  d.clearRect(0,0,DW,DH);
  const bmax = Math.max(B*2, 20);

# Order Completion versus Collision — a guided tour

> **The question.** Stage 1 of the elliptic curve method multiplies a point by a huge
> scalar built out of all the prime powers below a bound $B$. When it succeeds at a
> *small* bound, is that luck — a chance collision — or is it the point's order genuinely
> dividing the scalar, and doing so *early* in the run? This page answers that question
> and shows you the exact arithmetic behind it.

---

## 1. The object at the centre of everything

Stage 1 walks up the primes $2, 3, 5, 7, 11, \dots$ — we call this the **schedule** — and
after passing all primes up to a cutoff $C$ it has accumulated the scalar

$$k(B, C) \;=\; \prod_{\substack{q \le C\\ q \text{ prime}}} q^{\lfloor \log_q B\rfloor},
\qquad k(B) := k(B,B).$$

For $B = 10$ this is $k(10) = 2^3\cdot 3^2 \cdot 5 \cdot 7 = 2520$: every prime power that
fits under $10$.

The run "fires" on a point when the accumulated scalar annihilates it. Everything else on
this page follows from a single observation about when that happens.

<details>
<summary><b>Why the exponent is $\lfloor\log_q B\rfloor$ — click to expand</b></summary>

Stage 1 wants to kill any order all of whose prime powers are below $B$. The largest power
of $q$ that is at most $B$ is $q^{\lfloor \log_q B\rfloor}$, so including that one factor
covers every possible $q$-part of a $B$-powersmooth order. Including more would be waste;
including less would miss orders.
</details>

---

## 2. The event is a divisibility, not a coin flip

> **Firing Criterion.** A point of order $n$ is annihilated by $k(B,C)$ **exactly when**
> every prime $q$ dividing $n$ satisfies $q \le C$ *and* $q^{v_q(n)} \le B$. Taking
> $C = B$: the full stage-1 scalar kills the point exactly when $n$ is **$B$-powersmooth**.

Read that twice. There is no probability in it. Whatever randomness exists in ECM lives in
the *draw of the curve* — that is, in which group order you get — not in the success event
given that order.

<details>
<summary><b>Proof sketch</b></summary>

Divisibility $n \mid k$ is equivalent to $v_r(n) \le v_r(k)$ for every prime $r$. The
exponent of $r$ in $k(B,C)$ is $\lfloor\log_r B\rfloor$ if $r \le C$ and $0$ otherwise. So
the condition reads: $v_r(n) \le \lfloor \log_r B\rfloor$ for $r \le C$ — which is exactly
$r^{v_r(n)} \le B$ — and $v_r(n) = 0$ for $r > C$. $\blacksquare$
</details>

And the immediate corollary that powers the experimental control:

> **No order completion above the bound.** If the order has any prime factor exceeding
> $B$, stage 1 provably *never* fires on it. So at a factor of the modulus far larger than
> $B$, hits can only be collisions.

---

## 3. Play with it: the staircase

Here is the whole theory in one interactive picture. Choose an order $m$ and a bound $B$.
The widget computes — exactly, never by simulation — how many of the $m$ points fire, how
the count builds up as the schedule advances, how the rate responds to the bound, and how
the exact rate compares with the folklore collision baseline $1 - e^{-1.44B/m}$.

**Things to try.**
- Start at $m = 720$, $B = 10$. Notice the count goes $1 \to 8 \to 72 \to 360$ and then
  *stops*: the prime $7$ does nothing because $7 \nmid 720$.
- Slide $B$ from $10$ up to $60$ with $m$ fixed. The rate does not budge until $B$ reaches
  $16 = 2^4$ — the next prime power dividing $720$. That is the *no dose response* theorem
  in motion.
- Try $m = 65537$ (a prime) with $B = 200$. The count is $1$: only the identity fires. This
  is the control channel, exactly.
- Push $B$ to a few hundred with a composite $m$ and watch the pill list: nearly every
  prime in the schedule is grey, i.e. inert.

{{interactive_demo:0}}

---

## 4. Counting, exactly

> **Exact Rate.** A scalar $k$ annihilates exactly $\gcd(m,k)$ of the $m$ points of a
> cyclic group of order $m$. The success rate is exactly $\gcd(m,k)/m$.

> **The count is the powersmooth part.** $\gcd(m, k(B))$ is precisely the largest
> $B$-powersmooth divisor of $m$.

So "how often does stage 1 fire?" is literally "how big is the powersmooth part of the
order?" — a question of arithmetic, not of probability.

<details>
<summary><b>Proof sketch of the exact rate</b></summary>

Put $g=\gcd(m,k)$ and $d = m/g$. Since $m/g$ and $k/g$ are coprime, $m \mid ka$ holds iff
$d \mid a$. The multiples of $d$ below $m$ are $d\cdot 0, \dots, d\cdot (g-1)$: exactly $g$
of them. $\blacksquare$
</details>

Two more counts fall out immediately, and both matter in practice:

- **Several curves.** With $c$ independent points the number of tuples that fire at least
  once is *exactly* $m^c - (m - \gcd(m,k))^c$, so the rate is exactly $1-(1-\rho)^c$ with
  $\rho = \gcd(m,k)/m$. No independence assumption is needed; it is a count of a product set.
- **Real curves do better.** The group of points over a prime field is
  $\mathbb{Z}/m_1 \times \mathbb{Z}/m_2$, where the firing count is
  $\gcd(m_1,k)\gcd(m_2,k) \ge \gcd(m_1m_2, k)$. Splitting the order can only help.

---

## 5. The staircase, drawn

The next figure plots what the widget animates: on the left the cumulative count climbing
through the schedule and flattening; on the right the rate as a function of the bound, with
the collision baseline for comparison and dotted lines at the prime powers dividing $m$ —
the *only* places where the rate can possibly move.

{{visualization:0}}

> **Monotone, flat, saturating.** Raising the bound can only increase the count. It changes
> nothing unless some prime power dividing the order lies between the old and the new bound.
> And it reaches its maximum $m$ — every point fires — precisely when $m$ itself is
> $B$-powersmooth. Passing a prime $q$ multiplies the count by exactly
> $q^{\min(v_q(m),\,\lfloor \log_q B\rfloor)}$.

<details>
<summary><b>Why the "no dose response" proof works</b></summary>

The exponent of $r$ in $\gcd(m,k(B))$ is $\min(v_r(m), \lfloor\log_r B\rfloor)$ when
$r \le B$ and $0$ otherwise. The key elementary identity is that
$\min(v, \lfloor \log_r B\rfloor)$ is *the largest $j \le v$ with $r^j \le B$*. So if no
prime power $r^j$ with $j \le v_r(m)$ separates $B$ from $B'$, the two minima agree at every
prime, and the two gcds are equal. $\blacksquare$
</details>

To compute this efficiently you never form $k(B)$ — a number with astronomically many
digits. You climb the staircase with the jump formula instead:

{{algorithm:0}}

---

## 6. *Where* it fires: the sharpest statement on this page

> **The firing position is the largest prime factor.** For an order that fires at all, the
> least cutoff at which the accumulating scalar already kills it is *exactly* the largest
> prime factor of that order.

For a fixed order there is no distribution over positions at all: the position is
determined. A run fires within the first $\pi(L)$ of its $\pi(B)$ steps precisely when the
order has no prime factor above $L$, and conversely a late fire *certifies* a large prime
factor.

{{algorithm:1}}

And there is a purely structural reason the positions can never look uniform:

> **Sparsity.** The steps at which the count ever increases are exactly the primes dividing
> $m$ that are at most $B$ — at most $\omega(m) \le \log_2 m$ of the $\pi(B)$ steps. Once
> the schedule is longer than $\log_2 m$, some step never fires, so the distribution of
> firing positions cannot be uniform.

> **A long inert block.** A pigeonhole over the staircase gives a set of at least
> $\pi(B)/(\omega(m)+1)$ schedule primes carrying *one and the same* firing count. If the
> order has at most one prime divisor, at least half the schedule is inert.

The uniform distribution increases at every step; a block of that length that is exactly
flat is precisely the feature a goodness-of-fit test picks up. Here is the picture:

{{visualization:1}}

And here is the algorithm that extracts and certifies such a block:

{{algorithm:2}}

---

## 7. Against the folklore model

The traditional heuristic assigns a per-curve success chance $1 - e^{-1.44B/p}$. Since
$1 - e^{-x} \le x$ always, that baseline never exceeds $1.44 B/m$. So:

> **Order completion beats the baseline** whenever the powersmooth part of the order
> exceeds $1.44\,B$.

For $m = 720$, $B = 10$: the true rate is $1/2$, and the baseline is at most
$1.44\cdot 10/720 = 0.02$. A factor of more than $25$. Meanwhile in the control channel,
where every prime factor of the order exceeds the bound, the exact firing count collapses
to $1$ and the order-completion rate is precisely $1/m$ — which is why hits recorded there
measure the collision floor and nothing else.

Run the numbers yourself:

{{demo:0}}

---

## 8. Does the picture survive at larger scale?

It does, and for an arithmetic reason: **scale invariance** — multiplying the order by any
factor coprime to the scalar leaves the firing *count* unchanged. Growing the order dilutes
the rate through the denominator, but it cannot convert order completion into luck.

The final experiment samples random orders at two bit lengths, holds the smoothness
parameter fixed (so the budget scales with the target, as it must for the comparison to
mean anything), and reports the exact rates with confidence intervals at three doses:

{{demo:1}}

---

## 9. What is *not* proved, and why

Two honest limits, worth stating precisely.

<details>
<summary><b>A distributional early-fire theorem</b></summary>

"The median normalized firing position is at most $0.3$" cannot follow from arithmetic
alone. For a single order the position is deterministic, so a median statement is about a
*family* of orders — that is, about the distribution of largest prime factors of smooth
numbers, which is
[Dickman-function](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dickman_function) territory. What survives
unconditionally is the deterministic skeleton: everything but the large-prime part has
already fired by any cutoff you name.
</details>

<details>
<summary><b>A quantitative distance-to-uniform bound</b></summary>

We prove uniformity is impossible (support size $O(\log m)$) and that a flat block of length
$\pi(B)/(\omega(m)+1)$ exists. Turning length into a
[Kolmogorov–Smirnov](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kolmogorov%E2%80%93Smirnov_test)
sup-distance bound requires knowing *where* the block sits: a run at the boundary
contributes little, a run straddling the middle contributes about $\ell/(2\pi(B))$.
</details>

---

## 10. Takeaways

1. Stage-1 success is a **divisibility**: the order is $B$-powersmooth. Not a coin flip.
2. Its count is a **greatest common divisor** — the powersmooth part of the order.
3. Its dose response is a **saturating staircase**; flatness in the bound is the prediction,
   not an anomaly.
4. Its position in the schedule is the **largest prime factor** of the order, so the useful
   work is front-loaded and the positions can never be uniform.
5. The **collision heuristic is a floor**, dominated whenever the powersmooth part exceeds
   $1.44 B$.

Further reading: [Lenstra's elliptic curve factorization](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lenstra_elliptic-curve_factorization),
[smooth numbers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Smooth_number), and
[the prime-counting function](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prime-counting_function).

firing count `C ↦ gcd(m, k(B,C))` jumps exactly at the prime divisors of the order below
the bound, hence at most `ω(m)` times.  Here we draw the consequence that the

up; the quantitative sup-distance version is conjecture 1 of `FUTURE_DIRECTIONS.md`.
